analysis.one_liner: Forces the largest state-chartered banks to convert to federally regulated national banks.
analysis.headline: The bill received no cosponsors and died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the 2023 bank failures, Senator J.D. Vance proposed automatically converting every state-chartered bank with $100 billion or more in assets into a national bank. National banks are supervised by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, which generally applies stricter, more uniform rules than the state systems that had let banks like Silicon Valley Bank operate. The bill would have closed off a path large banks use to get lighter regulation. It attracted no cosponsors and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, it would have protected bank depositors and taxpayers by ensuring the largest banks are supervised by the stricter national bank regulator, reducing the chance a megabank fails and triggers a taxpayer-backed bailout.

how_it_helps.text: It automatically converts any state-chartered bank with $100 billion or more in assets into a national bank, so instead of being regulated by the Federal Reserve or the FDIC it would be supervised by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, a national banking regulator.

It aims to prevent banks from choosing or keeping a state charter that subjects them to lighter oversight as they grow past $100 billion in assets — the pattern associated with the 2023 failures of Silicon Valley Bank and First Republic, where state-chartered banks avoided the strictest rules applied to similarly sized national banks.

analysis.who_pays: Large banks would have borne the cost of converting to national charters and complying with the Comptroller of the Currency's stricter rules; some of that cost could be passed to customers through fees.

drawbacks.text: The OCC has historically been viewed as a more industry-friendly regulator than the Federal Reserve or FDIC; moving megabanks to national charters could concentrate supervision in one agency and shift chartering fees to the OCC, and critics of the bill's premise noted that the 2023 failures involved banks under a range of regulators.
Forcing a charter conversion by operation of law, rather than letting banks choose to apply, is a significant federal override of state banking authority and of banks' own chartering decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill never advanced, so there is no enacted benefit or cost to weigh. As a proposal, it offered a plausible regulatory fix — tighter, more uniform federal oversight for the largest banks — but had no bipartisan backing and died without debate, leaving the post-2023-bank-failure regulatory questions unaddressed by Congress.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Banking Committee, and sat there with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Vance introduced the bill on July 26, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the Banking Committee never took up the bill — there is no markup, hearing, or vote in the action history.
When the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, all bills not passed expired; S. 2497 was never reported out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks that preferred their lighter-touch state charters, since the stricter oversight the bill would have imposed never happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks preferring lighter state regulation

for.name: Sen. J.D. Vance
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put it before the Senate Banking Committee.

against.name: Large banks and banking industry groups
against.what_they_did: The bill's aim of stripping the largest banks of lighter state-charted regulation faced industry opposition; no banking trade group publicly supported it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had zero cosponsors from either party, so no party bloc ever took a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Very large banks ($100B+ in assets, roughly 15-20 institutions)
industries.note: Would have forced them out of state charters into national charters supervised by the OCC, closing off a route to lighter state-level regulation. Had the bill passed, it would have cost them regulatory flexibility and, in some cases, state-law business powers.

industries.industry: State banking regulators and the dual chartering system
industries.note: Would have removed the largest state-chartered banks from state supervision, shrinking the dual (state/federal) banking system's reach.
Would have handed the OCC supervisory authority over every $100B+ bank, expanding its jurisdiction and fee base.
